How to Search Public Records in Florida

Florida's Clerk of the Circuit Court handles both court files and official land records. Learn how business, court, and property searches work and how Chapter 119 applies to records requests.

Key takeaways

  • ✓The Clerk of the Circuit Court keeps both court files and the official land records in each county.
  • ✓Chapter 119 sets no fixed response deadline. Agencies must respond within a reasonable time.
  • ✓Sunbiz shows entity status, registered agent, and officers from annual reports.

In this guide

  1. Business Records: Sunbiz
  2. Court Records: the Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller
  3. Property Records: Appraiser, Clerk, and Tax Collector
  4. Florida's Public Records Law (Chapter 119)
  5. Tips for Florida Searches

Florida has 67 counties and a long tradition of open government. Two features set Florida apart for researchers: the county clerk often handles both court records and the official land records, and the state's public records law does not set a fixed number of days for agencies to respond. This guide explains where Florida records live and how to ask for what is not online.

Business Records: Sunbiz

Florida business entities are registered with the Division of Corporations of the Florida Department of State, and the public search site is known as Sunbiz. You can search by entity name, by registered agent or officer name, or by document number. An entity record shows the status, filing date, principal address, registered agent, and the officers or managers listed on the most recent annual report. Florida entities file annual reports, so the filing history is a useful way to see when a company last updated its information and whether it is active or administratively dissolved.

Court Records: the Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller

Each county has a Clerk of the Circuit Court, who is typically also the county comptroller. The clerk keeps records for circuit courts, which handle felonies and larger civil cases, and for county courts, which handle misdemeanors and smaller civil matters. Each clerk runs its own website and search system, so the tools differ from county to county. Some provide free docket search and paid document access, and some require registration for certain records.

  • Choose the county where the case was filed. Florida does not have a single free public search that covers every county.
  • Look for the case type (civil, criminal, traffic, probate, family) when a portal makes you choose a division.
  • Some records, such as certain family, juvenile, and sealed matters, are confidential and will not appear.

Federal cases are filed in the Northern, Middle, or Southern District of Florida and are searched through PACER.

Property Records: Appraiser, Clerk, and Tax Collector

  • County property appraiser: shows the owner of record, parcel number, exemptions such as homestead, and assessed values.
  • Clerk of the Circuit Court (Official Records): holds recorded deeds, mortgages, liens, and related documents. Most clerks provide an online index search.
  • County tax collector: shows tax bills, payments, and delinquent amounts.

When researching a property, look at the recorded documents for mortgages and releases, and search the clerk's civil records for foreclosure filings that name the property or the owner.

Florida's Public Records Law (Chapter 119)

The Florida Public Records Act is in Chapter 119 of the Florida Statutes and is reinforced by the Florida Constitution. It gives any person the right to inspect and copy records of state and local agencies at reasonable times and under reasonable conditions. Florida's law differs from many states in several ways.

  • No fixed deadline. Chapter 119 does not set a number of days for a response. Agencies must respond in good faith and within a reasonable time, and unreasonable delay can amount to an unlawful refusal.
  • No writing required. The law does not authorize an agency to insist on a written request, and you are generally not required to give your name or a reason.
  • Mediation is available. The Office of the Attorney General runs a voluntary public records mediation program for qualifying disputes.
  • Court is an option. Requesters can file a civil action, and attorney's fees can be assessed against an agency that violated the law.

Do not confuse Chapter 119 with the Sunshine Law, which governs open meetings of public boards. Both are often described together, but Chapter 119 is the one that covers records.

Tips for Florida Searches

  • Keep requests specific so the custodian can identify the records and estimate costs.
  • Because there is no deadline, send a polite follow-up if you have not heard back within a week or two and keep a record of each contact.
  • Expect exemptions. Florida has many statutory exemptions, and an agency should cite the specific exemption when it withholds or redacts a record.
  • Use the clerk's office for certified copies of court and land records.

Portals and procedures change, so confirm the current process with the office that holds the record.
